title: SNAT ephemeral port exhaustion causing transient cross-tenant packet misdelivery (production incident)
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Summary: Several Dedicated customers reported intermittent cross-tenant request failures and DNS mismatches during high outbound connection churn. Investigation showed transient packet misdelivery between tenant workloads caused by SNAT ephemeral port exhaustion and incorrect conntrack association after port recycling on shared host nodes.

Root cause: The node-level SNAT implementation used a global ephemeral port pool and aggressive port reuse heuristics under heavy connection churn. When the node exhausted ephemeral ports, the kernel/userland SNAT code recycled ports quickly and, under race conditions, conntrack entries were not consistently tied to tenant namespaces due to an oversight in our conntrack namespace tagging for tunneled overlay interfaces. The result: a small fraction of outbound replies returned with stale SNAT port mappings and were accepted by a different tenant's socket on the same host, causing transient cross-tenant traffic and DNS response confusion.

Scope and impact: High for affected clusters. Impact observed as: short-lived cross-tenant responses (seconds), occasional DNS response mismatches, and customer-facing request errors for a minority of requests. Customer impact: high for three enterprise customers running bursty export jobs; overall incidence rate <0.02% of outbound flows on peak nodes.

Immediate mitigations applied: 1) Increased ephemeral port range per-node to reduce immediate exhaustion. 2) Temporarily lowered SNAT port reuse aggressiveness (disabled fast-recycle path) via a hotpatch on affected hosts. 3) Rolled an emergency iptables/conntrack rule to prefer namespace-scoped conntrack lookups on overlay interfaces. These mitigations reduced incidents to zero within 45 minutes for impacted clusters.

Permanent fix implemented: 1) Implemented per-tenant reserved SNAT port ranges at the node agent level so tenants no longer compete for the same ephemeral pool. 2) Fixed conntrack namespace tagging for our Geneve/GRE overlay device code path so conntrack entries are always scoped to tenant namespaces. 3) Improved SNAT port pool allocator to prefer unused ports and back-off aggressive recycle heuristics. 4) Added health checks and telemetry for port exhaustion and conntrack namespace collisions.

Rollout strategy: Canary rollout across three dedicated clusters representing high-churn, medium-churn, and low-churn tenants. Monitor token-level egress errors, conntrack collision metrics, and DNS mismatch traces for 48 hours before wider rollout. Full rollout completed to all Dedicated clusters by 2025-10-06 with staged restarts to minimize disruption.

Testing and validation: Unit tests for allocator logic + integration tests simulating churned outbound connections across tenant namespaces. Load test harness reproduced exhaustion scenario; new allocator eliminated collisions in 10/10 runs. Post-deploy synthetic traffic and customer traffic telemetry validated no regression in latency or throughput.

Communication and follow-ups: Customer support notified impacted customers with incident timeline, causes, and recommended temporary mitigations they could apply (increase client-side idle timeouts). Internal incident postmortem created and linked below.

Trade-offs and notes: Per-tenant reserved SNAT ranges reduce maximum ephemeral ports available per-tenant but substantially increase isolation correctness. We documented knobs for very high-throughput tenants to request larger port ranges as part of Dedicated capacity planning.

Next actions: 1) Backfill OSS documentation and runbook for future SNAT exhaustion. 2) Add automated alerts for ephemeral port consumption > 70% per node. 3) Explore moving to per-tenant egress proxies for strong isolation (research item).
